blocks.text: The verb κεπφοῦσθαι [kepphousthai], formed from cepphus, means not only to be carried away and to be lightly driven about by every wind like a cepphus, but also to be easily deceived and lured with bait. So in Prov. VII, 22, of the heedless young man whom the adulteress has charmed with her enticements: Ὁ δὲ ἐπηκολούθησεν αὐτῇ κεπφωθείς [Ho de epēkolouthēsen autē kepphōtheis]; But he follows her, like a cepphus, easily driven, or easily deceived. Hesychius: Κεπφωθείς· ἐπαρθεὶς, ἀπατηθείς [Kepphōtheis; epartheis, apatētheis]; [col. 265] Carried away, deceived. And again, after Κέφαλον [Kephalon]: Κεπφωθεὶς, καταγελασθείς· εἴρηται δὲ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλόγου δίκην ἀνοήτως συνεπαγομένων [Kepphōtheis, katagelastheis; eirētai de epi tōn alogou dikēn anoētōs synepagomenōn]; Mocked: it is said of those who, like a brute beast, are foolishly led along. Suidas: Κεπφωθείς· ἐπαρθεὶς, ἐρεθισθεὶς, ὀξέως ἐλαυνόμενος [Kepphōtheis; epartheis, erethistheis, oxeōs elaunomenos]; Carried away, stirred up, swiftly driven. These are various interpretations of the same passage. But ἀπατηθεὶς [apatētheis] pleases me most. 1. Because in the passage we have cited κεπφωθεὶς [kepphōtheis] stands for the Hebrew פתאים, for which the Greeks read פתאים, that is, simple ones, εὐαπάτητοι [euapatētoi]. For it comes from the verb פתה, which they usually render ἀπατᾷν [apatan]. 2. Because the cepphus is a bird easily deceived, which boys, by offering it foam, draw to themselves without any trouble and catch by laying hands on it. Hence κέπφος [kepphos] is commonly used by the Greeks for a fool. Thus the proverb Κέπφος λάρος [Kepphos laros] strikes at the senseless man who is deceived by desire for anything and is caught. And in Aristophanes, in the Peace,

Καὶ κέπφοι τρήρωνες ἀλωπεκίδεσσι πέπεισθε [Kai kepphoi trērōnes alōpekidessi pepeisthe], [III, 4] And you cepphi and doves (that is, fools and simpletons) trust little foxes. And again in the Plutus, Ὦ κέπφε [Ō kepphe], O cepphus, that is, O fool. Accordingly, on the former passage the Scholiast says: Εὔηθες ζῶον ὁ κέπφος [Euēthes zōon ho kepphos], The cepphus is a foolish animal. And on the latter: Ὄρνεον γὰρ ἄφρον, ὅπερ φιλεῖ ἀφρὸν θαλάττιον ἐσθίειν. Τοῦτο βουλόμενοι οἱ τῶν ἁλιέων παῖδες χειρώσασθαι, ῥίπτουσι τὸ πρῶτον πόῤῥωθεν ἀφρὸν, εἶτα ἐγγύτατα, εἶτα φέρουσιν τοῦτο ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν, καὶ οὕτω κατὰ μικρὸν ἀπατῶντες, εὐχερῶς ἀγρεύουσι τοῦτο ἐμπεσὸν εἰς τὰς χεῖρας αὐτῶν· εἴληπται οὖν εἰς παροιμίαν ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλογίστων ἀνδρῶν, καὶ ἀνοήτων [Orneon gar aphron, hoper philei aphron thalattion esthiein. Touto boulomenoi hoi tōn halieōn paides cheirōsasthai, rhiptousi to prōton porrhōthen aphron, eita engytata, eita pherousin touto en tais chersin, kai houtō kata mikron apatōntes, eucherōs agreuousi touto empeson eis tas cheiras autōn; eilēptai oun eis paroimian epi tōn alogistōn andrōn, kai anoētōn]. For it is a foolish bird, which delights in eating sea foam. So when the fishermen's sons wish to catch it, they first throw foam from a distance, then nearer and nearer, afterwards they carry it in their hands, and so, luring it little by little, they easily catch it as it falls into their hands. Hence it has become a proverb for senseless and witless men. The older writers had reported this very thing about this bird. So the Philosopher, History of Animals, book 9, chapter 35: Οἱ δὲ κέπφοι ἁλίσκονται τῷ ἀφρῷ, κόπτουσι γὰρ αὐτόν· διὸ προσραίνοντες θηρεύουσιν [Hoi de kepphoi haliskontai tō aphrō, koptousi gar auton; dio prosrainontes thēreuousin]. The cepphi are caught with foam, for they go after it; therefore they hunt them by throwing foam at them. And Nicander, Alexipharmaca, verse 165:

Ἀφρὸν ἐπεγκεράσοιο θοοῦ δορπήϊα κέπφου. Τῷ γὰρ δὴ ζωήν τε σαοῖ, καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖ. Εὖτε δόλοις νήχοντα κακοφθόρα τέκν᾽ ἁλιήων Οἰωνὸν χραίνωσιν. ὁ δ᾽ ἐς χέρας ἔμπεσε παίδων, Θηρεύων ἀφροῖο νέην κλύδα λευκαίνουσαν. [Aphron epenkerasoio thoou dorpēia kepphou. Tō gar dē zōēn te saoi, kai potmon epispei. Eute dolois nēchonta kakophthora tekn᾽ haliēōn Oiōnon chrainōsin. ho d᾽ es cheras empese paidōn, Thēreuōn aphroio neēn klyda leukainousan.]

Mix in foam, the food of the swift cepphus. For by it the bird both preserves its life and brings on its doom, when the destructive sons of fishermen craftily spatter the swimming bird with it. And it falls into the boys' hands, chasing the fresh white spray of foam. See more in the Scholiast on Nicander, Hesychius, Suidas, the Etymologicum ^{(2)} and others, whom I have no time to copy out now. Nor is there need, since they merely repeat what has already been said. I will only note that in these words of Hesychius and Suidas, Κεπφωθεὶς· ἐπαρθεὶς [Kepphōtheis; epartheis], one should read ἐπαχθεὶς [epachtheis] instead of ἐπαρθεὶς [epartheis]. For on Hesychius's own authority Κεπφωθεὶς [Kepphōtheis] is said ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλόγου δίκην ἀνοήτως συνεπαγομένων [epi tōn alogou dikēn anoētōs synepagomenōn], of those who are foolishly led along like a brute beast.
